entries.062ec6527dd44627cea4c91d69f3b655e8a2bb4a: <div sID="gen10495" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="10" osisID="Ps.10" sID="Ps.10"/> <div eID="gen10495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10496" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10497" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint translation joins this psalm with the ninth, and makes them but one; but the Hebrew makes it a distinct psalm, and the scope and style are certainly different. In this psalm, I. David complains of the wickedness of the wicked, describes the dreadful pitch of impiety at which they had arrived (to the great dishonour of God and the prejudice of his church and people), and notices the delay of God's appearing against them, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1-Ps.10.11">ver. 1-11</reference>. II. He prays to God to appear against them for the relief of his people and comforts himself with hopes that he would do so in due time, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.12-Ps.10.18">ver. 12-18</reference>.
entries.3e38dc8513f514501007d4d92a0db51f993a3a6a: <div eID="gen10497" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10496" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Character of the Wicked; The Character of Persecutors.</title> <div sID="gen10498" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Why standest thou afar off, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ? <hi type="italic">why</hi> hidest thou <hi type="italic">thyself</hi> in times of trouble? <hi type="super">2</hi> The wicked in <hi type="italic">his</hi> pride doth persecute the poor: let them be taken in the devices that they have imagined. <hi type="super">3</hi> For the wicked boasteth of his heart's desire, and blesseth the covetous, <hi type="italic">whom</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> abhorreth. <hi type="super">4</hi> The wicked, through the pride of his countenance, will not seek <hi type="italic">after God:</hi> God <hi type="italic">is</hi> not in all his thoughts. <hi type="super">5</hi> His ways are always grievous; thy judgments <hi type="italic">are</hi> far above out of his sight: <hi type="italic">as for</hi> all his enemies, he puffeth at them. <hi type="super">6</hi> He hath said in his heart, I shall not be moved: for <hi type="italic">I shall</hi> never <hi type="italic">be</hi> in adversity. <hi type="super">7</hi> His mouth is full of cursing and deceit and fraud: under his tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> mischief and vanity. 8 He sitteth in the lurking places of the villages: in the secret places doth he murder the innocent: his eyes are privily set against the poor. <hi type="super">9</hi> He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den: he lieth in wait to catch the poor: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net. <hi type="super">10</hi> He croucheth, <hi type="italic">and</hi> humbleth himself, that the poor may fall by his strong ones. <hi type="super">11</hi> He hath said in his heart, God hath forgotten: he hideth his face; he will never see <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <div eID="gen10498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10499" type="x-p"/> David, in these verses, discovers, <div eID="gen10499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10500" type="x-p"/> I. A very great affection to God and his favour; for, in the time of trouble, that which he complains of most feelingly is God's withdrawing his gracious presence (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Why standest thou afar off,</hi> as one unconcerned in the indignities done to thy name and the injuries done to the people?" Note, God's withdrawings are very grievous to his people at any time, but especially in times of trouble. Outward deliverance is afar off and is hidden from us, and then we think God is afar off and we therefore want inward comfort; but that is our own fault; it is because we judge by outward appearance; we stand afar off from God by our unbelief, and then we complain that God stands afar off from us. <div eID="gen10500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10501" type="x-p"/> II. A very great indignation against sin, the sins that made the times perilous, <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1">2 Tim. iii. 1</reference>. he beholds the transgressors and is grieved, is amazed, and brings to his heavenly Father their evil report, not in a way of vain-glory, boasting before God that he was not as <hi type="italic">these publicans</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Luke xviii. 11</reference>), much less venting any personal resentments, piques, or passions, of his own; but as one that laid to he art that which is offensive to God and all good men, and earnestly desired a reformation of manners. Passionate and satirical invectives against bad men do more hurt than good; if we will speak of their badness, let it be to God in prayer, for he alone can make them better. This long representation of the wickedness of the wicked is here summed up in the first words of it (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">The wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor,</hi> where two things are laid to their charge, pride and persecution, the former the cause of the latter. Proud men will have all about them to be of their mind, of their religion, to say as they say, to submit to their dominion, and acquiesce in their dictates; and those that either eclipse them or will not yield to them they malign and hate with an inveterate hatred. Tyranny, both in state and church, owes its origin to pride. The psalmist, having begun this description, presently inserts a short prayer, a prayer in a parenthesis, which is an advantage and no prejudice to the sense: <hi type="italic">Let them be taken,</hi> as proud people often are, <hi type="italic">in the devices that they have imagined,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">v. 2</reference>. Let their counsels be turned headlong, and let them fall headlong by them. These two heads of the charge are here enlarged upon. <div eID="gen10501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10502" type="x-p"/> 1. They are proud, very proud, and extremely conceited of themselves; justly therefore did he wonder that God did not speedily appear against them, for he hates pride, and resists the proud. (1.) The sinner proudly glories in his power and success. He <hi type="italic">boasts of his heart's desire,</hi> boasts that he can do what he pleases (as if God himself could not control him) and that he has all he wished for and has carried his point. Ephraim said, <hi type="italic">I have become rich, I have found me out substance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Hos. xii. 8</reference>. "Now, Lord, is it for thy glory to suffer a sinful man thus to pretend to the sovereignty and felicity of a God?" (2.) He proudly contradicts the judgment of God, which, we are sure, is according to truth; for he <hi type="italic">blesses the covetous, whom the Lord abhors.</hi> See how God and men differ in their sentiments of persons: God abhors covetous worldlings, who make money their God and idolize it; he looks upon them as his enemies, and will have no communion with them. <hi type="italic">The friendship of the world is enmity to God.</hi> But proud persecutors bless them, and approve their sayings, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.13">Ps. xlix. 13</reference>. They applaud those as wise whom God pronounces foolish (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>); they justify those as innocent whom God condemns as deeply guilty before him; and they admire those as happy, in having their portion in this life, whom God declares, upon that account, truly miserable. <hi type="italic">Thou, in thy lifetime, receivedst thy good things.</hi> (3.) He proudly casts off the thoughts of God, and all dependence upon him and devotion to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The wicked, through the pride of his countenance,</hi> that pride of his heart which appears in his very countenance (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.17">Prov. vi. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">will not seek after God,</hi> nor entertain the thoughts of him. <hi type="italic">God is not in all his thoughts,</hi> not in any of them. <hi type="italic">All his thoughts are that there is not God.</hi> See here, [1.] The nature of impiety and irreligion; it is <hi type="italic">not seeking after God</hi> and <hi type="italic">not having him in our thoughts.</hi> There is no enquiry made after him (<reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job xxxv. 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.6">Jer. ii. 6</reference>), no desire towards him, no communion with him, but a secret wish to have no dependence upon him and not to be beholden to him. Wicked people will not seek after God (that is, will not call upon him); they live without prayer, and that is living without God. They have many thoughts, many projects and devices, but no eye to God in any of them, no submission to his will nor aim at his glory. [2.] The cause of this impiety and irreligion; and that is pride. Men will not seek after God because they think they have no need of him, their own hands are sufficient for them; they think it a thing below them to be religious, because religious people are few, and mean, and despised, and the restraints of religion will be a disparagement to them. (4.) He proudly makes light of God's commandments and judgments (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">His wings are always grievous;</hi> he is very daring and resolute in his sinful courses; he will have his way, though ever so tiresome to himself and vexatious to others; he travails with pain in his wicked courses, and yet his pride makes him wilful and obstinate in them. God's judgments (what he commands and what he threatens for the breach of his commands) are <hi type="italic">far above out of his sight;</hi> he is not sensible of his duty by the law of God nor of his danger by the wrath and curse of God. Tell him of God's authority over him, he turns it off with this, that he never saw God and therefore does not know that there is a God, he is <hi type="italic">in the height of heaven,</hi> and <hi type="italic">quæ supra nos nihil ad nos—we have nothing to do with things above us.</hi> Tell him of God's judgments which will be executed upon those that go on still in their trespasses, and he will not be convinced that there is any reality in them; they are <hi type="italic">far above out of his sight,</hi> and therefore he thinks they are mere bugbears. (5.) He proudly despises all his enemies, and looks upon them with the utmost disdain; he puffs at those whom God is preparing to be a scourge and ruin to him, as if he could baffle them all, and was able to make his part good with them. But, as it is impolitic to despise an enemy, so it is impious to despise any instrument of God's wrath. (6.) He proudly sets trouble at defiance and is confident of the continuance of his own prosperity (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He hath said in his heart,</hi> and pleased himself with the thought, <hi type="italic">I shall not be moved,</hi> my goods are laid up for many years, and <hi type="italic">I shall never be in adversity;</hi> like Babylon, that said, <hi type="italic">I shall be a lady for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.47.7">Isa. xlvii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.7">Rev. xviii. 7</reference>. Those are nearest ruin who thus set it furthest from them. <div eID="gen10502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10503" type="x-p"/> 2. They are persecutors, cruel persecutors. For the gratifying of their pride and covetousness, and in opposition to God and religion, they are very oppressive to all within their reach. Observe, concerning these persecutors, (1.) That they are very bitter and malicious (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">His mouth is full of cursing.</hi> Those he cannot do a real mischief to, yet he will spit his venom at, and breathe out the slaughter which he cannot execute. Thus have God's faithful worshippers been anathematized and cursed, with bell, book, and candle. Where there is a heart full of malice there is commonly a mouth full of curses. (2.) They are very false and treacherous. There is mischief designed, but it is hidden under the tongue, not to be discerned, for <hi type="italic">his mouth is full of deceit</hi> and vanity. He has learned of the devil to deceive, and so to destroy; with this his hatred is covered, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.26">Prov. xxvi. 26</reference>. He cares not what lies he tells, not what oaths he breaks, nor what arts of dissimulation he uses, to compass his ends. (3.) That they are very cunning and crafty in carrying on their designs. They have ways and means to concert what they intend, that they may the more effectually accomplish it. Like Esau, that cunning hunter, <hi type="italic">he sits in the lurking places, in the secret places,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his eyes are privily set</hi> to do mischief (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">v. 8</reference>), not because he is ashamed of what he does (if he blushed, there were some hopes he would repent), not because he is afraid of the wrath of God, for he imagines God will never call him to an account (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">v. 11</reference>), but because he is afraid lest the discovery of his designs should be the breaking of them. Perhaps it refers particularly to robbers and highwaymen, who lie in wait for honest travellers, to make a prey of them and what they have. (4.) That they are very cruel and barbarous. Their malice is against <hi type="italic">the innocent,</hi> who never provoked them—against <hi type="italic">the poor,</hi> who cannot resist them and over whom it will be no glory to triumph. Those are perfectly lost to all honesty and honour against whose mischievous designs neither innocence nor poverty will be any man's security. Those that have power ought to protect the innocent and provide for the poor; yet these will be the destroyers of those whose guardians they ought to be. And what do they aim at? It is to <hi type="italic">catch the poor,</hi> and <hi type="italic">draw them into their net,</hi> that is, get them into their power, not to strip them only, but to <hi type="italic">murder them.</hi> They hunt for the precious life. It is God's poor people that they are persecuting, against whom they bear a mortal hatred for his sake whose they are and whose image they bear, and therefore they lie in wait to murder them: <hi type="italic">He lies in wait as a lion</hi> that thirsts after blood, and feeds with pleasure upon the prey. The devil, whose agent he is, is compared to a roaring lion that seeks not what, but whom, he may devour. (5.) That they are base and hypocritical (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">He crouches and humbles himself,</hi> as beasts of prey do, that they may get their prey within their reach. This intimates that the sordid spirits of persecutors and oppressors will stoop to any thing, though ever so mean, for the compassing of their wicked designs; witness the scandalous practices of Saul when he hunted David. It intimates, likewise, that they cover their malicious designs with the pretence of meekness and humility, and kindness to those they design the greatest mischief to; they seem to humble themselves to take cognizance of the poor, and concern themselves in their concernments, when it is in order to make them fall, to make a prey of them. (6.) That they are very impious and atheistical, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">v. 11</reference>. They could not thus break through all the laws of justice and goodness towards man if they had not first shaken off all sense of religion, and risen up in rebellion against the light of its most sacred and self-evident principles: <hi type="italic">He hath said in his heart, God has forgotten.</hi> When his own conscience rebuked him with the consequences of it, and asked how he would answer it to the righteous Judge of heaven and earth, he turned it off with this, <hi type="italic">God has forsaken the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.12">Ezek. viii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.9">ix. 9</reference>. This is a blasphemous reproach, [1.] Upon God's omniscience and providence, as if he could not, or did not, see what men do in this lower world. [2.] Upon his holiness and the rectitude of his nature, as if, though he did see, yet he did not dislike, but was willing to connive at, the most unnatural and inhuman villanies. [3.] Upon his justice and the equity of his government, as if, though he did see and dislike the wickedness of the wicked, yet he would never reckon with them, nor punish them for it, either because he could not or durst not, or because he was not inclined to do so. Let those that suffer by proud oppressors hope that God will, in due time, appear for them; for those that are abusive to them are abusive to God Almighty too. <div eID="gen10503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10504" type="x-p"/> In singing this psalm and praying it over, we should have our hearts much affected with a holy indignation at the wickedness of the oppressors, a tender compassion of the miseries of the oppressed, and a pious zeal for the glory and honour of God, with a firm belief that he will, in due time, give redress to the injured and reckon with the injurious.
entries.3a48eac05307ec8b1ac6fa42afbafbb1c251ec53: <div eID="gen10504" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer against Persecutors.</title> <div sID="gen10505" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Arise, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; O God, lift up thine hand: forget not the humble. <hi type="super">13</hi> Wherefore doth the wicked contemn God? he hath said in his heart, Thou wilt not require <hi type="italic">it.</hi> <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou hast seen <hi type="italic">it;</hi> for thou beholdest mischief and spite, to requite <hi type="italic">it</hi> with thy hand: the poor committeth himself unto thee; thou art the helper of the fatherless. <hi type="super">15</hi> Break thou the arm of the wicked and the evil <hi type="italic">man:</hi> seek out his wickedness <hi type="italic">till</hi> thou find none. <hi type="super">16</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> King for ever and ever: the heathen are perished out of his land. <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , thou hast heard the desire of the humble: thou wilt prepare their heart, thou wilt cause thine ear to hear: 18 To judge the fatherless and the oppressed, that the man of the earth may no more oppress. <div eID="gen10505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10506" type="x-p"/> David here, upon the foregoing representation of the inhumanity and impiety of the oppressors, grounds an address to God, wherein observe, <div eID="gen10506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10507" type="x-p"/> I. What he prays for. 1. That God would himself appear (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Arise, O Lord! O God! lift up thy hand,</hi> manifest thy presence and providence in the affairs of this lower world. <hi type="italic">Arise, O Lord!</hi> to the confusion of those who say that thou hidest thy face. Manifest thy power, exert it for the maintaining of thy own cause, lift up thy hand to give a fatal blow to these oppressors; let thy everlasting arm be made bare." 2. That he would appear for his people: "<hi type="italic">Forget not the humble, the afflicted,</hi> that are poor, that are made poorer, and are poor in spirit. Their oppressors, in their presumption, say that thou hast forgotten them; and they, in their despair, are ready to say the same. Lord, make it to appear that they are both mistaken." 3. That he would appear against their persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) That he would disable them from doing any mischief: <hi type="italic">Break thou the arm of the wicked,</hi> take away his power, <hi type="italic">that the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.34.30">Job xxxiv. 30</reference>. We read of oppressors whose dominion was taken away, but their lives were prolonged (<reference osisRef="Dan.7.12">Dan. vii. 12</reference>), that they might have time to repent. (2.) That he would deal with them for the mischief they had done: "<hi type="italic">Seek out his wickedness;</hi> let that be all brought to light which he thought should for ever lie undiscovered; let that be all brought to account which he thought should for ever go unpunished; bring it out <hi type="italic">till thou find none,</hi> that is, till none of his evil deeds remain unreckoned for, none of his evil designs undefeated, and none of his partisans undestroyed." <div eID="gen10507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10508" type="x-p"/> II. What he pleads for the encouraging of his own faith in these petitions. <div eID="gen10508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10509" type="x-p"/> 1. He pleads the great affronts which these proud oppressors put upon God himself: "Lord, it is thy own cause that we beg thou wouldst appear in; the enemies have made it so, and therefore it is not for thy glory to let them go unpunished" (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Wherefore do the wicked contemn God?</hi> He does so; for he says, "<hi type="italic">Thou wilt not require it;</hi> thou wilt never call us to an account for what we do," than which they could not put a greater indignity upon the righteous God. The psalmist here speaks with astonishment, (1.) At the wickedness of the wicked: "Why do they speak so impiously, why so absurdly?" It is a great trouble to good men to think what contempt is cast upon the holy God by the sin of sinners, upon his precepts, his promises, his threatenings, his favours, his judgments; all are despised and made light of. <hi type="italic">Wherefore do the wicked thus contemn God?</hi> It is because they do not know him. (2.) At the patience and forbearance of God towards them: "Why are they suffered thus to contemn God? Why does he not immediately vindicate himself and take vengeance on them?" It is because the day of reckoning is yet to come, when the measure of their iniquity is full. <div eID="gen10509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10510" type="x-p"/> 2. He pleads the notice God took of the impiety and iniquity of these oppressors (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">v. 14</reference>): "Do the persecutors encourage themselves with a groundless fancy that thou wilt never see it? Let the persecuted encourage themselves with a well-grounded faith, not only that thou hast seen it, but that thou doest behold it, even all the mischief that is done by the hands, and all the spite and malice that lurk in the hearts, of these oppressors; it is all known to thee, and observed by thee; nay, not only thou hast seen it and dost behold it, but thou wilt requite it, wilt recompense it into their bosoms, by thy just and avenging hand." <div eID="gen10510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10511" type="x-p"/> 3. He pleads the dependence which the oppressed had upon him: "<hi type="italic">The poor commits himself unto thee,</hi> each of them does so, I among the rest. They rely on thee as their patron and protector, they refer themselves to thee as their Judge, in whose determination they acquiesce and at whose disposal they are willing to be. <hi type="italic">They leave themselves with thee</hi>" (so some read it), "not prescribing, but subscribing, to thy wisdom and will. They thus give thee honour as much as their oppressors dishonour thee. They are thy willing subjects, and put themselves under thy protection; therefore protect them." <div eID="gen10511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10512" type="x-p"/> 4. He pleads the relation in which God is pleased to stand to us, (1.) As a great God. He <hi type="italic">is King for ever and ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.10.16">v. 16</reference>. And it is the office of a king to administer justice for the restraint and terror of evil-doers and the protection and praise of those that do well. To whom should the injured subjects appeal but to the sovereign? <hi type="italic">Help, my Lord, O King! Avenge me of my adversary.</hi> "Lord, let all that pay homage and tribute to thee as their King have the benefit of thy government and find thee their refuge. Thou art an everlasting King, which no earthly prince is, and therefore canst and wilt, by an eternal judgment, dispense rewards and punishments in an everlasting state, when time shall be no more; and to that judgment the poor refer themselves." (2.) As a good God. He is the helper of the fatherless (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">v. 14</reference>), of those who have no one else to help them and have many to injure them. He has appointed kings to <hi type="italic">defend the poor and fatherless</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.3">Ps. lxxxii. 3</reference>), and therefore much more will he do so himself; for he has taken it among the titles of his honour to be a Father to the fatherless (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">Ps. lxviii. 5</reference>), a helper of the helpless. <div eID="gen10512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10513" type="x-p"/> 5. He pleads the experience which God's church and people had had of God's readiness to appear for them. (1.) He had dispersed and extirpated their enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.16">v. 16</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The heathen have perished out of his land;</hi> the remainders of the Canaanites, the seven devoted nations, which have long been as thorns in the eyes and goads in the sides of Israel, are now, at length, utterly rooted out; and this is an encouragement to us to hope that God will, in like manner, break the arm of the oppressive Israelites, who were, in some respects, worse than heathens." (2.) He had heard and answered their prayers (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Lord, thou hast</hi> many a time <hi type="italic">heard the desire of the humble,</hi> and never saidst to a distressed suppliant, <hi type="italic">Seek in vain.</hi> Why may not we hope for the continuance and repetition of the wonders, the favours, which our father told us of?" <div eID="gen10513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10514" type="x-p"/> 6. He pleads their expectations from God pursuant to their experience of him: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast heard,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">thou will cause thy ear to hear,</hi> as, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.9">Ps. vi. 9</reference>. Thou art the same, and thy power, and promise, and relation to thy people are the same, and the work and workings of grace are the same in them; why therefore may we not hope that he who has been will still be, will ever be, a God hearing prayers?" But observe, (1.) In what method God hears prayer. He first prepares the heart of his people and then gives them an answer of peace; nor may we expect his gracious answer, but in this way; so that God's working upon us is the best earnest of his working for us. He prepares the heart for prayer by kindling holy desires, and strengthening our most holy faith, fixing the thoughts and raising the affections, and then he graciously accepts the prayer; he prepares the heart for the mercy itself that is wanting and prayed for, makes us fit to receive it and use it well, and then gives it in to us. The preparation of the heart is from the Lord, and we must seek unto him for it (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.1">Prov. xvi. 1</reference>) and take that as a leading favour. (2.) What he will do in answer to prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">v. 18</reference>. [1.] He will plead the cause of the persecuted, will judge the fatherless and oppressed, will judge for them, clear up their innocency, restore their comforts, and recompense them for all the loss and damage they have sustained. [2.] He will put an end to the fury of the persecutors. Hitherto they shall come, but no further; here shall the proud waves of their malice be stayed; an effectual course shall be taken <hi type="italic">that the man of the earth may no more oppress.</hi> See how light the psalmist now makes of the power of that proud persecutor whom he had been describing in this psalm, and how slightly he speaks of him now that he had been considering God's sovereignty. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is but <hi type="italic">a man of the earth,</hi> a man <hi type="italic">out of</hi> the earth (so the word is), sprung out of the earth, and therefore mean, and weak, and hastening to the earth again. Why then should we be afraid of the fury of the oppressor when he is but <hi type="italic">man that shall die, a son of man that shall be as grass?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa. li. 12</reference>. He that protects us is the Lord of heaven; he that persecutes us is but a man of the earth. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God has him in a chain, and can easily restrain the remainder of his wrath, so that he cannot do what he would. When God speaks the word Satan shall by his instruments no more deceive (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.3">Rev. xx. 3</reference>), no more oppress. <div eID="gen10514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10515" type="x-p"/> In singing <reference osisRef="Ps.10.12-Ps.10.18">these verses</reference> we must commit religion's just but injured cause to God, as those that are heartily concerned for its honour and interests, believing that he will, in due time, plead it with jealousy.  <chapter eID="Ps.10"/> <div eID="gen10515" type="x-p"/>

entries.12d5ebb768e78971880327677384e1f6a37209d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5545"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 10</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.10.1-Ps.10.18">Psa 10:1-18</reference>. The Psalmist mourns God's apparent indifference to his troubles, which are aggravated by the successful malice, blasphemy, pride, deceit, and profanity of the wicked. On the just and discriminating providence of God he relies for the destruction of their false security, and the defense of the needy.</title> <div sID="gen8418" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5545"/>1. These are, of course, figurative terms (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.7.6">Psa 7:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.13.1">13:1</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen8418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8419" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hidest--</hi>Supply "thine eyes" or "face." <div eID="gen8419" type="x-p"/>
entries.f870143f6603368244e694b665b9cb3c6d050130: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5546"/><div sID="gen8420" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5546"/>2. Literally, "In pride of the wicked they (the poor or humble, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Psa 10:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.12.5">12:5</reference>) shall be taken in the devices they (the proud) have imagined." <div eID="gen8420" type="x-p"/>
entries.fd1655c40799066e32b323d7936daf9a910cb476: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5547"/><div sID="gen8421" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5547"/><hi type="bold">3. heart's--</hi>or, "soul's."<div eID="gen8421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">desire--</hi>that is, his success in evil.<div eID="gen8422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and blesseth, &c.--</hi>he (the wicked) blesseth the covetous, he despiseth the Lord. <div eID="gen8423" type="x-p"/>
entries.1915eadef25055a00d3065c233d7aa970d4233e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5548"/><div sID="gen8424" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5548"/>4. The face expresses the self-conceit, whose fruit is practical atheism (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>). <div eID="gen8424" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d48667a827d72f2e88e8e563dd77b60b1594962: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5549"/><div sID="gen8425" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5549"/>5-6. Such is his confidence in the permanence of his way or course of life, that he disregards God's providential government (out of sight, because he will not look, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Is 26:11</reference>), sneers at his enemies, and boasts perpetual freedom from evil. <div eID="gen8425" type="x-p"/>
entries.78fddb0e45c226ec25b431bc1a8b037ebd445e74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5550"/><div sID="gen8426" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5550"/>7-10. The malignity and deceit (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.3">Psa 140:3</reference>) of such are followed by acts combining cunning, fraud, and violence (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pr 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">18</reference>), aptly illustrated by the habits of the lion, and of hunters taking their prey. "Poor," in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">Psa 10:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">10, 14</reference>, represents a word peculiar to this Psalm, meaning the sad or sorrowful; in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">Psa 10:9</reference>, as usual, it means the pious or meek sufferer. <div eID="gen8426" type="x-p"/>
entries.cbf22ff17cf1e37a034cb8389e83ed7fc8561855: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5553"/><div sID="gen8430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5553"/>11. As before, such conduct implies disbelief or disregard of God's government. <div eID="gen8430" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7167401bb55a669af9a097ece6be1cf8f78a0af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5554"/><div sID="gen8431" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5554"/>12. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.19">Psa 9:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.7">3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen8431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the humble--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17">Psa 10:17</reference>, and Margin.)<div eID="gen8432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8433" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lift up thine hand--</hi>exert thy power. <div eID="gen8433" type="x-p"/>
entries.03451986b7724d20d0e7cd29278786ad15ea0e41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5555"/><div sID="gen8434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5555"/>13-14. It is in vain to suppose God will overlook sin, however forbearing; for He carefully examines or beholds all wickedness, and will mark it by His providential (Thine hand) punishment. <div eID="gen8434" type="x-p"/>
entries.7c83c37dc897aa9a0331c1cac35bbd6970bec43b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5557"/><div sID="gen8437" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5557"/><hi type="bold">15. arm--</hi>power.<div eID="gen8437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8438" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">till thou find none--</hi>So far from not requiting (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.13">13</reference>), God will utterly destroy the wicked and his deeds (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.16">34:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">37:36</reference>). <div eID="gen8438" type="x-p"/>
entries.e81bfa8db30d022945b517cdb4cf47b26d89df09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5558"/><div sID="gen8439" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5558"/>16-18. God reigns. The wicked, if for a time successful, shall be cut off. He hears and confirms the hearts of His suffering people (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.7">Psa 112:7</reference>), executes justice for the feeble, and represses the pride and violence of conceited, though frail, men (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.16">Psa 9:16</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.10"/>

entries.13bc464827a3d4b606bdafc0ca7fc3a3229dfce1: <div eID="gen18597" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18599" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18598" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18600" type="x-p"/> The psalmist complains to God of the oppressions which the poor suffer from the wicked man, whom he describes as the hater of the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>; proud, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.3">Psa 10:3</reference>; one who will not seek God, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>; and is regardless of his judgments, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.5">Psa 10:5</reference>; self-confident, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.6">Psa 10:6</reference>; blasphemous and deceitful, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference>; strives by subtlety and treachery to destroy the poor, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.8-Psa.10.10">Psa 10:8-10</reference>; and supposes that God is regardless of his conduct, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.11">Psa 10:11</reference>. The psalmist calls earnestly on God to preserve the poor and humble, and cast down the oppressor, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.12-Psa.10.15">Psa 10:12-15</reference>. He foresees that his prayer is heard; that judgment will be executed, and the poor delivered, <reference osisRef="Psa.10.16-Psa.10.18">Psa 10:16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen18600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18601" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18602" type="x-p"/> Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? - This Psalm makes a part of the preceding in the Vulgate and Septuagint; and in four of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. It seems to belong to the time of the captivity, or the return of the captives. It was probably made in reference to Sanballat, and the other enemies or the Jews. There is a great similarity between this and <reference osisRef="Psa.13.1-Psa.13.6">Psa 13:1-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.14.1-Psa.14.7">Psa 14:1-7</reference>, 35, and <reference osisRef="Psa.53.1-Psa.53.6">Psa 53:1-6</reference> : In these, as Calmet remarks, we find the same complaints, the same sentiments, and almost the same expressions. <div eID="gen18602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18603" type="x-p"/> God is represented here as standing at some distance, beholding the oppression of his people, and yet apparently disregarding it.
entries.534291b8f99043e5019af604a929c17ff2029235: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18604" type="x-p"/> The wicked in his pride - On no principle of nature or reason can we account for a wicked man persecuting a humble follower of God because of his religion. The devil hates godliness; and the wicked man hates it also because the devil is in his heart.
entries.7b30c81a186d6668aa3956c43812ebe252f81830: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18605" type="x-p"/> Boasteth of his heart's desire - Boasts among his fellows how often he has gratified such and such passions, in such and such circumstances. This shows the excess of a depraved and imbruted spirit. He who can boast of his iniquity, is in the broad road to perdition. Should such a one repent and turn to God, it would be equal to any miracle. <div eID="gen18605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18606" type="x-p"/> Blesseth the covetous, whom the Lord abhorreth - Or, he blesseth the covetous, he abhorreth the Lord. Those who are like himself he commends, and with them he associates; and they abhor the Lord - they have a mortal hatred against every thing that is holy; and they are under the full influence of that carnal mind which is enmity to the Lord.
entries.b087e22c15d17d5700c12317fddeca02225c0775: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18607" type="x-p"/> Will not seek after God - He is too proud to bend his knee before his Judge; he is too haughty to put on sackcloth, and lay himself in the dust, though without deep repentance and humiliation he must without doubt perish everlastingly.
entries.b6731ea877ad9fcc4c38ff661ae4217fba75b365: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18608" type="x-p"/> His ways are always grievous - Or, He is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times. He is full of lust, or irregular and unholy desires; he conceives and brings forth sin; and sin being finished, time, place, and opportunity concurring, death is soon brought forth. <div eID="gen18608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> Thy judgments are far above out of his sight - He is so blinded with sin, that he cannot see the operations of God's hand. <div eID="gen18609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18610" type="x-p"/> He puffeth at them - He whistles at them; insults God, and despises men. He overthrows them with his breath; he has only to give orders, and they are destroyed. "Bring me the head of Giaffer," said an Asiatic despot. The head was immediately brought! No trial, no judge, no jury; but the despot's will and caprice.
entries.8bf43082d86eb9c330348bf11f86eec94e18c8c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18611" type="x-p"/> I shall not be moved - I have whatever I covet. I hold whatsoever I have gotten. I have money and goods to procure me every gratification.
entries.e9c814c2d3bc9614b7fcff554f82142158b4727a: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18612" type="x-p"/> His mouth is full of cursing, and deceit, and fraud - What a finished character! A blasphemer, a deceitful man, and a knave!
entries.620b47712fdbc8cfe73d82fcd8089dfdf6c9261e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18613" type="x-p"/> He sitteth in the lurking places - In this and the following verse there appears to be an allusion to espionage, or setting of spies on a man's conduct; or to the conduct of an assassin or private murderer. He sitteth in lurking places - in secret places; his eyes - spies - are privily set; he lieth in wait secretly: he doth catch the poor, when he draweth him into his net. He is like a hunter that lays his traps and gins, digs his pits, sets his nets; and when the prey falls into them, he destroys its life.
entries.86d447617e47e33b1a0d3693b0b6b457ec7c9889: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18614" type="x-p"/> He croucheth - Of the scoffing, mocking, insulting, and insidious conduct of Sanballat, Tobiah, and Geshem, the fourth and sixth chapters of Nehemiah give abundant proof; and possibly the allusion is to them. The lion squats down and gathers himself together, that he may make the greater spring.
entries.26174ea7d442beacb3dfe3636f8a877147f3ed5e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18615" type="x-p"/> God hath forgotten - He hath cast off this people, and he will never more re-establish them. So Sanballat thought.
entries.66d73da3363f97a7db584884ab0ebe871d8661c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen18615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18616" type="x-p"/> Arise, O Lord - Hear their reproaches see their guile, consider thy oppressed people. "Lift up thine hand," threaten them, that they may desist and repent. If they repent not let them be punished.
entries.e364956877082dec1f4b0507226133dd7d79d625: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen18616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18617" type="x-p"/> Wherefore doth the tacked contemn God? - How is it that the Lord permits such persons to triumph in their iniquity? The longsuffering of God leadeth them to repentance.
entries.505088c192bea0100828a5f80a361e0c4fca59d0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen18617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18618" type="x-p"/> Thou hast seen it - Nothing can escape thy notice. Thou hast not forgotten thy justice, though judgment is not speedily executed on an evil work. But thou wilt requite it with thy hand. By thy power thou wilt cast down and destroy the wicked. <div eID="gen18618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18619" type="x-p"/> The poor committeth himself unto thee - To thee he has given up his body, his soul, and his cause; with the full conviction that thou who art the helper of fatherless, will not forget him.
entries.6fc87a115d8ab291d717534225fda8daf4f146aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen18619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18620" type="x-p"/> Break thou the arm - Destroy his power, deprive him of his influence, that he may be no longer able to oppress. <div eID="gen18620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18621" type="x-p"/> Seek out his wickedness till thou find none - All his public haunts and private ways shall be investigated; thou wilt bring all his villanies to light, and continue to inflict punishment, while there is a crime to punish. Or, "Continue to judge and punish transgressors, till not one is to be found." This agrees with the following verse.
entries.48a9ea63471a3124882e9cbdc5d2a1e3c11751fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen18621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18622" type="x-p"/> The Lord is king for ever - He has, and ever will have, the supreme power. <div eID="gen18622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18623" type="x-p"/> The heathen are perished out of his land - They are all either cut off or converted. This may refer to the Canaanites. What a mercy that we can say this of our own country! Once it was entirely heathen; now not one heathen family in the whole land.
entries.2aa70464979828e5af204a3377fd433e33adf96a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen18623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18624" type="x-p"/> Lord, thou hast heard - Thou hast not permitted thy tempted and afflicted followers to pray in vain. <div eID="gen18624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18625" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt prepare their heart - See the economy of the grace of God: <div eID="gen18625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18626" type="x-p"/> 1. God prepares the heart; <div eID="gen18626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18627" type="x-p"/> 2. Suggests the prayer; <div eID="gen18627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18628" type="x-p"/> 3. Hears what is prayed; <div eID="gen18628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18629" type="x-p"/> 4. Answers the petition. <div eID="gen18629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18630" type="x-p"/> He who has got a cry in his heart after God, may rest assured that that cry proceeded from a Divine preparation, and that an answer will soon arrive. No man ever had a cry in his heart after salvation, but from God. He who continues to cry shall infallibly be heard.
entries.d97fd413e5217e89af31dee5e11e88142d282444: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen18630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18631" type="x-p"/> That the man of the earth may no more oppress - I believe the Hebrew will be better translated thus: "That he may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land." Destroy the influence of the tyrant; and let him not have it again in his power to add even one additional act of oppression to those which he has already committed. <div eID="gen18631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18632" type="x-p"/> How many for the sake of their religion, and because they would serve God with a pure conscience, have, by wicked lords, proud and arrogant land owners, been driven off their farms, turned out of their houses, deprived of their employments, and exposed to wretchedness! While they served the devil, and were regardless of their souls, they had quiet and peaceable possession; but when they turned to the Lord, and became sober and industrious, attended the means of grace, read their Bible, and were frequent in prayer, then the vile man of the earth drove them from their dwellings! In the sight of such Philistines, piety towards God is the highest of crimes. What a dreadful account must these give to the Judge of the Fatherless and the oppressed!  <chapter eID="Ps.10"/> <div eID="gen18632" type="x-p"/>

entries.b7f407e014ece5559488d9b3e2d5df5c078b9ec3: <div eID="gen9117" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Plaintive and Supplicatory Prayer under the Pressure of Heathenish Foes at Home and Abroad</title> <div sID="gen9118" type="x-p"/> This Psalm and Ps 33 are the only ones that are anonymous in the First book of the Psalms. But Ps 10 has something peculiar about it. The lxx gives it with Ps 9 as one Psalm, and not without a certain amount of warrant for so doing. Both are laid out in tetrastichs; only in the middle portion of Ps 10 some three line strophes are mixed with the four line. And assuming that the ק-strophe, with which Ps 9 closes, stands in the place of a כ-strophe which one would look for after the י-strophe, then Ps 10, beginning with ל, continues the order of the letters. At any rate it begins in the middle of the alphabet, whereas Ps 9 begins at the beginning. It is true the ל-strophe is then followed by strophes without the letters that come next in order; but their number exactly corresponds to the letters between ל and ק, ר, שׁ, ת with which the last four strophes of the Psalm begin, viz., six, corresponding to the letters מ, נ, ס, ע, פ, צ, which are not introduced acrostically. In addition to this it is to be remarked that Ps 9 and <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference> are most intimately related to one another by the occurrence of rare expressions, as לעתּות בצּרה and דּך; by the use of words in the same sense, as אנושׁ and גּוים; by striking thoughts, as “Jahve doth not forget” and “Arise;” and by similarities of style, as the use of the <hi type="italic">oratio directa</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">obliqua</hi>, Ps 9:21; Psa 10:13. And yet it is impossible that the two Psalms should be only one. Notwithstanding all their community of character they are also radically different. Ps 9 is a thanksgiving Psalm, Ps 10 is a supplicatory Psalm. In the latter the personality of the psalmist, which is prominent in the former, keeps entirely in the background. The enemies whose defeat Ps 9 celebrates with thanksgiving and towards whose final removal it looks forward are גּוים, therefore foreign foes; whereas in Ps 10 apostates and persecutors of his own nation stand in the foreground, and the גוים are only mentioned in the last two strophes. In their form also the two Psalms differ insofar as Ps 10 has no musical mark defining its use, and the tetrastich strophe structure of Ps 9, as we have already observed, is not carried out with the same consistency in Ps 10. And is anything really wanting to the perfect unity of Ps 9? If it is connected with Ps 10 and they are read together <hi type="italic">uno tenore</hi>, then the latter becomes a tail-piece which disfigures the whole. There are only two things possible: Ps 10 is a pendant to Ps 9 composed either by David himself, or by some other poet, and closely allied to it by its continuance of the alphabetical order. But the possibility of the latter becomes very slight when we consider that Ps 10 is not inferior to Ps 9 in the antiquity of the language and the characteristic nature of the thoughts. Accordingly the mutual coincidences point to the same author, and the two Psalms must be regarded as “two co-ordinate halves of one whole, which make a higher unity” (Hitz.). That hard, dull, and tersely laconic language of deep-seated indignation at moral abominations for which the language has, as it were, no one word, we detect also elsewhere in some Psalms of David and of his time, those Psalms, which we are accustomed to designate as Psalms written in the indignant style (<hi type="italic">in grollendem Stil</hi>).
entries.f0ae2db9f72a4d80f20bc8daf7475dd6fc3f5b3f: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1-Ps.10.2">Psa 10:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen9118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9119" type="x-p"/> The Psalm opens with the plaintive inquiry, why Jahve tarries in the deliverance of His oppressed people. It is not a complaining murmuring at the delay that is expressed by the question, but an ardent desire that God may not delay to act as it becomes His nature and His promise. למּה, which belongs to both members of the sentence, has the accent on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, as e.g., before עזבתּני in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.2">Psa 22:2</reference>, and before הרעתה in <reference osisRef="Exod.5.22">Exo 5:22</reference>, in order that neither of the two gutturals, pointed with <hi type="italic">a</hi>, should be lost to the ear in rapid speaking (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference>, and Luzzatto on <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa 11:2</reference>, נחה עליו).<note placement="foot">According to the Masora למּה without <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. is always <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> with the single exception of <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>, and ימּה with <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. is <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>; but, when the following closely connected word begins with one of the letters אהע it becomes <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, with five exceptions, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">Psa 49:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.15">1Sa 28:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.31">2Sa 14:31</reference> (three instances in which the guttural of the second word has the vowel i), and <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.22">2Sa 2:22</reference>, and Jer 15:18. In the Babylonian system of pointing, למה is always written without <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. and with the accent on the penultimate, vid., Pinsker, <hi type="italic">Einleitung in das Babylonish-hebräishce Punktationssystem</hi>, S. 182-184.</note> <div eID="gen9119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9120" type="x-p"/> For according to the primitive pronunciation (even before the Masoretic) it is to be read: <hi type="italic">lam h Adonaj</hi>; so that consequently ה and א are coincident. The poet asks why in the present hopeless condition of affairs (on בצּרה vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>) Jahve stands in the distance (בּרחוק, only here, instead of מרחוק), as an idle spectator, and why does He cover (תּעלּים with orthophonic <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi>, in order that it may not be pronounced תּעלים), viz., His eyes, so as not to see the desperate condition of His people, or also His ears (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.56">Lam 3:56</reference>) so as not to hear their supplication. For by the insolent treatment of the ungodly the poor burns with fear (Ges., Stier, Hupf.), not vexation (Hengst.). The assault is a πύρωσις, 1Pe 4:12. The verb דּלק which calls to mind דּלּקת, πυρετός, is perhaps chosen with reference to the heat of feeling under oppression, which is the result of the persecution, of the (בּו) דּלק אחריו of the ungodly. There is no harshness in the transition from the singular to the plural, because עני and רשׁע are individualising designations of two different classes of men. The subject to יתּפשׁוּ is the עניּים, and the subject to חשׁבוּ is the רשׁעים. The futures describe what usually takes place. Those who, apart from this, are afflicted are held ensnared in the crafty and malicious devices which the ungodly have contrived and plotted against them, without being able to disentangle themselves. The punctuation, which places <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> by זוּ, mistakes the relative and interprets it: “in the plots there, which they have devised.”
entries.d630648322b584baa6ca9bbc786cd4a5ef303776: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3-Ps.10.4">Psa 10:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen9120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9121" type="x-p"/> The prominent features of the situation are supported by a detailed description. The <hi type="italic">praett</hi>. express those features of their character that have become a matter of actual experience. הלּל, to praise aloud, generally with the <hi type="italic">accus</hi>., is here used with על of the thing which calls forth praise. Far from hiding the shameful desire or passion (<reference osisRef="Ps.112.10">Psa 112:10</reference>) of his soul, he makes it an object and ground of high and sounding praise, imagining himself to be above all restraint human or divine. Hupfeld translates wrongly: “and he blesses the plunderer, he blasphemes Jahve.” But the רשׁע who persecutes the godly, is himself a בּצע a covetous or rapacious person; for such is the designation (elsewhere with בּצע <reference osisRef="Prov.1.19">Pro 1:19</reference>, or רע בּצע <reference osisRef="Hab.2.9">Hab 2:9</reference>) not merely of one who “cuts off” (Arab. <hi type="italic">bḍ‛</hi>), i.e., obtains unjust gain, by trading, but also by plunder, πλεονέκτης. The verb בּרך (here in connection with <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, as in Num 23:20 with <hi type="italic">Tiphcha</hi> בּרך) never directly signifies <hi type="italic">maledicere</hi> in biblical Hebrew as it does in the alter Talmudic (whence בּרכּת השּׁם blasphemy<hi type="italic">, B. Sanhedrin 56a</hi>, and frequently), but to take leave of any one with a benediction, and then to bid farewell, to dismiss, to decline and abandon generally, <reference osisRef="Job.1.5">Job 1:5</reference>, and frequently (cf. the word <hi type="italic">remercier, abdanken</hi>; and the phrase “<hi type="italic">das Zeitliche segnen</hi>” = to depart this life). The declaration without a conjunction is climactic, like <reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.5">Amo 4:5</reference>; Jer 15:7. נאץ, properly to prick, sting, is sued of utter rejection by word and deed.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> stands between נאץ and יהוה, because to blaspheme God is a terrible thought and not to be spoken of without hesitancy, cf. the <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18">Psa 74:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.89.52">Psa 89:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.24">Isa 37:24</reference> (2Ki 19:23).</note> <div eID="gen9121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>, “the evil-doer according to his haughtiness” (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.18">Pro 16:18</reference>) is <hi type="italic">nom. absol</hi>., and בּל־ידרשׁ אין אלהים (contrary to the accentuation) is virtually the predicate to כּל־מזמּותיו. This word, which denotes the intrigues of the ungodly, in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.2">Psa 10:2</reference>, has in this verse, the general meaning: thoughts (from זמם, Arab. <hi type="italic">zmm</hi>, to join, combine), but not without being easily associated with the secondary idea of that which is subtly devised. The whole texture of his thoughts is, i.e., proceeds from and tends towards the thought, that he (viz., Jahve, whom he does not like to name) will punish with nothing (בּל the strongest form of subjective negation), that in fact there is no God at all. This second follows from the first; for to deny the existence of a living, acting, all-punishing (in one word: a personal) God, is equivalent to denying the existence of any real and true God whatever (Ewald).
entries.e74ef8c26e183ee5199921a60dfc828e7df1b4cc: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.5">Psa 10:5</reference> <div eID="gen9122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9123" type="x-p"/> This strophe, consisting of only three lines, describes his happiness which he allows nothing to disturb. The signification: to be lasting (prop. stiff, strong) is secured to the verb חיל (whence חיל) by Job 20:21. He takes whatever ways he chooses, they always lead to the desired end; he stands fast, he neither stumbles nor goes astray, cf. Jer 12:1. The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> דרכו (דּרכו) has no other meaning than that give to it by the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">Psa 24:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.58.8">Psa 58:8</reference>). Whatever might cast a cloud over his happiness does not trouble him: neither the judgments of God, which are removed high as the heavens out of his sight, and consequently do not disturb his conscience (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference>; and the opposite, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.23">Psa 18:23</reference>), nor his adversaries whom he bloweth upon contemptuously. מרום is the predicate: <hi type="italic">altissime remota</hi>. And הפיח בּ, to breathe upon, does not in any case signify: actually to blow away or down (to express which נשׁב or נשׁף would be used), but either to “snub,” or, what is more appropriate to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.10.5">Psa 10:5</reference></hi>, to blow upon them disdainfully, to puff at them, like הפּיח in Mal 1:13, and <hi type="italic">flare rosas</hi> (to despise the roses) in Prudentius. The meaning is not that he drives his enemies away without much difficulty, but that by his proud and haughty bearing he gives them to understand how little they interfere with him.
entries.e9c351650c85b082834755e9a8858b1dd4769db6: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.6-Ps.10.7">Psa 10:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen9123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9124" type="x-p"/> Then in his boundless carnal security he gives free course to his wicked tongue. That which the believer can say by reason of his fellowship with God, בּל־אמּוט (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.7">Psa 30:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Psa 16:8</reference>), is said by him in godless self-confidence. He looks upon himself in age after age, i.e., in the endless future, as אשׁר לא ברע, i.e., as one who (אשׁר as in <reference osisRef="Isa.8.20">Isa 8:20</reference>) will never be in evil case (ברע as in <reference osisRef="Exod.5.19">Exo 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.8">2Sa 16:8</reference>). It might perhaps also be interpreted according to Zec 8:20, Zec 8:23 (vid., Köhler, <hi type="italic">in loc</hi>.): in all time to come (it will come to pass) that I am not in misfortune. But then the personal pronoun (אני or הוּא) ought not be omitted; whereas with our interpretation it is supplied from אמּוט, and there is no need to supply anything if the clause is taken as an apposition: in all time to come he who.... In connection with such unbounded self-confidence his mouth is full of אלה, cursing, <hi type="italic">execratio</hi> (not perjury, <hi type="italic">perjurium</hi>, a meaning the word never has), מרמות, deceit and craft of every kind, and תּך, oppression, violence. And that which he has under his tongue, and consequently always in readiness for being put forth (<reference osisRef="Ps.140.4">Psa 140:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.66.17">Psa 66:17</reference>), is trouble for others, and in itself matured wickedness. Paul has made use of this <reference osisRef="Ps.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference> in his contemplative description of the corruptness of mankind, Rom 3:14.
entries.ac4d9fb19958f3b16b99aaf04528eb2645cd1f7b: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">Psa 10:8</reference> <div eID="gen9124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9125" type="x-p"/> The ungodly is described as a lier in wait; and one is reminded by it of such a state of anarchy, as that described in Hos 6:9 for instance. The picture fixes upon one simple feature in which the meanness of the ungodly culminates; and it is possible that it is intended to be taken as emblematical rather than literally. חצר (from חצר to surround, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">hdr , hṣr</hi>, and especially <hi type="italic">hdr</hi>) is a farm premises walled in (Arab. <hi type="italic">hadar , hadâr , hadâra</hi>), then losing the special characteristic of being walled round it comes to mean generally a settled abode (with a house of clay or stone) in opposition to a roaming life in tents (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.25.31">Lev 25:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.25.16">Gen 25:16</reference>). In such a place where men are more sure of falling into his hands than in the open plain, he lies in wait (ישׁב, like Arab. <hi type="italic">q‛d lh , subsedit = insidiatus est ei</hi>), murders unobserved him who had never provoked his vengeance, and his eyes להלכה יצפּנוּ. צפה to spie, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32">Psa 37:32</reference>, might have been used instead of צפן; but צפן also obtains the meaning, to lie in ambush (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.18">Pro 1:18</reference>) from the primary notion of restraining one’s self (Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍfn , fut. i</hi>. in Beduin Arabic: to keep still, to be immoveably lost in thought, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.24.1">Job 24:1</reference>), which takes a transitive turn in צפן “to conceal.” חלכה, the dative of the object, is pointed just as though it came from חיל: Thy host, i.e., Thy church, O Jahve. The pausal form accordingly is חלכה with <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>, not with <hi type="italic">Ṣere</hi> as in incorrect editions. And the appeal against this interpretation, which is found in the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. חלכאים <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">Psa 10:10</reference>, is set aside by the fact that this plural is taken as a double word: host (חל = חיל = חיל as in Oba 1:20) of the troubled ones (כּאים, not as Ben-Labrat supposes, for נכאים, but from כּאה weary, and mellow and decayed), as the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> (which is followed by the Syriac version) and the Masora direct, and accordingly it is pointed חלכּאים with <hi type="italic">Ṣere</hi>. The punctuation therefore sets aside a word which was unintelligible to it, and cannot be binding on us. There is a verb הלך, which, it is true, does not occur in the Old Testament, but in the Arabic, from the root Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥk , firmus fuit, firmum fecit</hi> (whence also Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥkl</hi>, intrans. to be firm, <hi type="italic">fermé</hi>, i.e., closed), it gains the signification in reference to colour: to be dark (cognate with חכל, whence חכלילי) and is also transferred to the gloom and blackness of misfortune.<note placement="foot">Cf. Samachschari’s <hi type="italic">Golden Necklaces</hi>, Proverb 67, which Fleischer translates: “Which is blacker: the plumage of the raven, which is black as coal, or thy life, O stranger among strangers?” The word “blacker” is here expressed by Arab. <hi type="italic">ahlaku</hi>, just as the verb Arab. <hi type="italic">halika</hi>, with its infinitives <hi type="italic">halak</hi> or <hi type="italic">hulkat</hi> and its derivatives is applied to sorrow and misery.</note> <div eID="gen9125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9126" type="x-p"/> From this an abstract is formed חלך or חלך (like חפשׁ): blackness, misfortune, or also of a defective development of the senses: imbecility; and from this an adjective חלכּה = חלכּי, or also (cf. חפשׁי, עלפּה <reference osisRef="Ezek.31.15">Eze 31:15</reference> = one in a condition of languishing, עלף) חלכּה = חלכּי, <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. חלכּאים, after the form דּוּדאים, from דּוּדי, Ew. §189, g.
entries.e2e54ca2840c1573364494fb1f26985aa3ba3673: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.9">Psa 10:9</reference> <div eID="gen9126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9127" type="x-p"/> The picture of the רשׁע, who is become as it were a beast of prey, is now worked out further. The <hi type="italic">lustrum</hi> of the lion is called סך <reference osisRef="Jer.25.38">Jer 25:38</reference>, or סכּה <reference osisRef="Job.38.40">Job 38:40</reference> : a thicket, from סכך, which means both to interweave and to plait over = to cover (without any connection with שׂך a thorn, Arab. <hi type="italic">shôk</hi>, a thistle). The figure of the lion is reversed in the second line, the עני himself being compared to the beast of prey and the רשׁע to a hunter who drives him into the pit-fall and when he has fallen in hastens to drag him away (משׁך, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">Psa 28:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.22">Job 24:22</reference>) in, or by means of (Hos 11:4, <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference>), his net, in which he has become entangled.
entries.9e203f3f858269bd7f22bbb28459f1a5325e7492: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10-Ps.10.11">Psa 10:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen9127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9128" type="x-p"/> The comparison to the lion is still in force here and the description recurs to its commencement in the second strophe, by tracing back the persecution of the ungodly to its final cause. Instead of the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> ודכה (ודכה <hi type="italic">perf. consec.</hi>), the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> reads ידכּה more in accordance with the Hebrew use of the tenses. <reference osisRef="Job.38.40">Job 38:40</reference> is the rule for the interpretation. The two futures depict the settled and familiar lying in wait of the plunderer. True, the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> דּכה in the signification “to crouch down” finds no support elsewhere; but the Arab. <hi type="italic">dakka</hi> to make even (cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">rṣd , firmiter inhaesit loco</hi>, of the crouching down of beasts of prey, of hunters, and of foes) and the Arab. <hi type="italic">dagga</hi>, compared by Hitzig, to move stealthily along, to creep, and <hi type="italic">dugjeh</hi> a hunter’s hiding-place exhibit synonymous significations. The ταπεινώσει αὐτὸν of the lxx is not far out of the way. And one can still discern in it the assumption that the text is to be read ישׁח ודכה: and crushed he sinks (Aquila: ὁ δὲ λασθεὶς καμφθήσεται); but even דּכה is not found elsewhere, and if the poet meant that, why could he not have written דּכה? (cf. moreover Jdg 5:27). If דּכה is taken in the sense of a position in which one is the least likely to be seen, then the first two verbs refer to the sculker, but the third according to the usual <hi type="italic">schema</hi> (as e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.124.5">Psa 124:5</reference>) is the predicate to חלכּאים (חלכּאים) going before it. Crouching down as low as possible he lies on the watch, and the feeble and defenceless fall into his strong ones, עצוּמיו, i.e., claws. Thus the ungodly slays the righteous, thinking within himself: God has forgotten, He has hidden His face, i.e., He does not concern Himself about these poor creatures and does not wish to know anything about them (the denial of the truth expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.9.13">Psa 9:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.19">Psa 9:19</reference>); He has in fact never been one who sees, and never will be. These two thoughts are blended; עב with the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Job.21.3">Job 21:3</reference>, and the addition of לנצח (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.7">Psa 94:7</reference>) denies the possibility of God seeing now any more than formerly, as being an absolute absurdity. The thought of a personal God would disturb the ungodly in his doings, he therefore prefers to deny His existence, and thinks: there is only fate and fate is blind, only an absolute and it has no eyes, only a notion and that cannot interfere in the affairs of men.
entries.ac3281607ea9cf6d74355fb37e7a449795580d25: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.12-Ps.10.13">Psa 10:12-13</reference> <div eID="gen9128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9129" type="x-p"/> The six strophes, in which the consecutive letters from מ to צ are wanting, are completed, and now the acrostic strophes begin again with ק. In contrast to those who have no God, or only a lifeless idol, the psalmist calls upon his God, the living God, to destroy the appearance that He is not an omniscient Being, by arising to action. We have more than one name of God used here; אל is a vocative just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.83.2">Psa 83:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, Psa 139:23. He is to lift up His hand in order to help and to punish (נשׂא יד, whence comes the <hi type="italic">imperat</hi>. נשׂא = שׂא, cf. נסה <reference osisRef="Ps.4.7">Psa 4:7</reference>, like שׁלח יד <reference osisRef="Ps.138.7">Psa 138:7</reference> and נטה יד <reference osisRef="Exod.7.5">Exo 7:5</reference> elsewhere). Forget not is equivalent to: fulfil the לא שׁכח of <reference osisRef="Ps.9.13">Psa 9:13</reference>, put to shame the שׁכח אל of the ungodly, Psa 10:11! Our translation follows the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> ענוים. That which is complained of in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.3">Psa 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference> is put in the form of a question to God in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.13">Psa 10:13</reference> : wherefore (על־מה, instead of which we find על־מה in Num 22:32; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.11">Jer 9:11</reference>, because the following words begin with letters of a different class) does it come to pass, i.e., is it permitted to come to pass? On the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. in this interrogative clause vid., Psa 11:3. מדּוּע inquires the cause, למּה the aim, and על־מה the motive, or in general the reason: on what ground, since God’s holiness can suffer no injury to His honour? On לא תדרשׁ with כּי, the <hi type="italic">oratio directa</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">obliqua</hi>, vid., on Ps 9:21.
entries.af2ea679045a890db7c35c1ec31731bf50b73b4e: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference> <div eID="gen9129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9130" type="x-p"/> Now comes the confirmation of his cry to God: It is with Him entirely different from what the ungodly imagine. They think that He will not punish; but He does see (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.22">2Ch 24:22</reference>), and the psalmist knows and confesses it: ראתה (defective = ראיתה <reference osisRef="Ps.35.22">Psa 35:22</reference>), Thou hast seen and dost see what is done to Thine own, what is done to the innocent. This he supports by a conclusion <hi type="italic">a genere ad speciem</hi> thus: the trouble which is prepared for others, and the sorrow (כּעס, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.3">Ecc 7:3</reference>) which they cause them, does not escape the all-seeing eye of God, He notes it all, to give it into (lay it in) His hand. “To give anything into any one’s hand” is equivalent to, into his power (1Ki 20:28, and frequently); but here God gives (lays) the things which are not to be administered, but requited, into His own hand. The expression is meant to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Ps.56.9">Psa 56:9</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.49.16">Isa 49:16</reference> : He is observant of the afflictions of His saints, laying them up in His hand and preserving them there in order, in His own time, to restore them to His saints in joy, and to their enemies in punishment. Thus, therefore, the feeble and helpless (read חלכּה or חלכּה; according to the Masoretic text חלכה Thy host, not חלכה, which is contrary to the character of the form, as pausal form for חלכה) can leave to Him, viz., all his burden (יהבו, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>), everything that vexes and disquiets him. Jahve has been and will be the Helper of the fatherless. יתום stands prominent by way of emphasis, like אותם <reference osisRef="Ps.9.13">Psa 9:13</reference>, and Bakius rightly remarks in <hi type="italic">voce pupilli synecdoche est, complectens omnes illos, qui humanis praesidiis destituuntur.</hi>
entries.1c6f95b92f41f5ce9622bd018024d9bfdf7f0a65: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.15-Ps.10.16">Psa 10:15-16</reference> <div eID="gen9130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9131" type="x-p"/> The desire for Jahve’s interposition now rises again with fresh earnestness. It is a mistake to regard דּרשׁ and מצא as correlative notions. In the phrase to seek and not find, when used of that which has totally disappeared, we never have דּרשׁ, but always בּקּשׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">Psa 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.12">Isa 41:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.20">Jer 50:20</reference>, and frequently. The verb דּרשׁ signifies here exactly the same as in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.13">Psa 10:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.9.13">Psa 9:13</reference> : “and the wicked<hi type="italic">(nom. absol</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.4">Psa 10:4</reference>) - mayst Thou punish his wickedness, mayst Thou find nothing more of it.” It is not without a meaning that, instead of the form of expression usual elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.36">Psa 37:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.8">Job 20:8</reference>), the address to Jahve is retained: that which is no longer visible to the eye of God, not merely of man, has absolutely vanished out of existence. This absolute conquest of evil is to be as surely looked for, as that Jahve’s universal kingship, which has been an element of the creed of God’s people ever since the call and redemption of Israel (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.18">Exo 15:18</reference>), cannot remain without being perfectly and visibly realised. His absolute and eternal kingship must at length be realised, even in all the universality and endless duration foretold in Zec 14:9; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>, Rev 11:15. Losing himself in the contemplation of this kingship, and beholding the kingdom of God, the kingdom of good, as realised, the psalmist’s vision stretches beyond the foes of the church at home to its foes in general; and, inasmuch as the heathen in Israel and the heathen world outside of Israel are blended together into one to his mind, he comprehends them all in the collective name of גּוים, and sees the land of Jahve (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.23">Lev 25:23</reference>), the holy land, purified of all oppressors hostile to the church and its God. It is the same that is foretold by Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.1">Isa 52:1</reference>), Nahum (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference>), and in other passages, which, by the anticipation of faith, here stands before the mind of the suppliant as an accomplished fact - viz. the consummation of the judgment, which has been celebrated in the hymnic half (Ps 9) of this double Psalm as a judgment already executed in part.
entries.8942ebd98a1f9230048626b4625dbb91de6b55d2: <reference osisRef="Ps.10.17-Ps.10.18">Psa 10:17-18</reference> <div eID="gen9131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9132" type="x-p"/> Still standing on this eminence from which he seems to behold the end, the poet basks in the realisation of that which has been obtained in answer to prayer.
